text.p: The coalition government of the Baltic state of Estonia was close to collapse on Monday as its two leading parties faced off over a controversial cooperation deal with the leading opposition party.

The right-wing Reform Party gave its government partner the Coalition Party a deadline of November 20 to cancel a deal it signed last week with the leading opposition party, the Centre Party, or it will consider leaving the government.
The fragile coalition was formed one year ago as the sixth government of Estonia since it quit the former Soviet Union in 1991. It also includes a bloc of small rural parties.
"We proposed to the Coalition Party that it cancel the agreement with the Centre Party, which we consider to be unethical," Reform Party party head Siim Kallas told Estonian radio.
As political parties gathered for emergency talks, Kallas said the deal must be cancelled by November 20 or the Reform Party leaders would meet to discuss leaving the government.
The agreement is a wide-ranging cooperation deal and was seen as a huge slap in the face to the Reform Party.
But the Coalition Party seemed unlikely to fall in with the Reformists' demands.
"It is unlikely that the agreement will be cancelled," Maart Siiman, Coalition Party parliamentary faction head, told the radio.
The current coalition has been beset by problems from the start, as the Reform Party favours more radical free market policies than the more cautious Coalition Party.
But tensions reached a peak during recent local government elections when the two parties campaigned against each other amid much mud-slinging.

The Coalition Party used to rule in alliance with the Centre Party but that government collapsed amid scandal after Centre Party leader Edgar Savisaar was found to have taped confidential conversations with leading politicians.
